First, we must define the concept of the best thing as a functional baseline for any given task, which is typically the maximization of perfection or the absolute peak efficiency of quality. Then we recognize that finding the absolute best version of something often follows the law of diminishing returns, where each incremental improvement requires an exponentially greater amount of time, money, or cognitive energy. We can see that at a certain point, the cost of reaching perfection begins to outweigh the actual value gained from that extra effort. This means that if spending ten more hours researching a single project only improves its performance by one percent, the pursuit of excellence becomes a form of procrastination rather than a choice of excellence. Next, we should consider the opportunity cost, which involves choosing the best possible option versus settling for something that works when the time spent optimizing is better used elsewhere. We also observe that in many real - world scenarios, such as software development or creative writing, being first or being timely is critical because a working solution allows for immediate feedback and iteration. Therefore, it is good enough to pick something that works whenever the marginal benefit of further optimization exceeds the marginal utility provided by that refinement. Finally, we conclude that choosing the working option over the perfect option is the superior strategy when speed, resource management, and the ability to move on to the next important task are more valuable than the theoretical ideal.
